answer_shown: Half-grown or fully grown caterpillars are easiest to identify. The larvae are generally characterized by 3 yellow stripes on the back, followed by a black, then a yellow stripe on the side. Look out for four dark spots forming a square on the second to last segment. Each spot has a short bristle (hair). The head is dark; it shows a typical upside down Y-shaped pale marking on the front. [S1][S3]
Eggs are pale green or white at the beginning, get covered in scales, and turn clear brown to brown before hatching [S2]. They hatch within 2-3 days [S2][S4].

The moth is 3 to 4 cm wide. Its front wings are dark brown while the rear wings are grey white [S2].

100-200 eggs are generally laid on the underside of the leaves typically near the base of the plant, close to the junction of the leaf and the stem [S2]. When populations are high eggs may be laid higher up the plants or on nearby vegetation [S2].

Small see-through patches on young maize leaves are windowing caused by early instars of Fall Armyworm. After hatching young caterpillars feed superficially, usually on the undersides of leaves, and feeding results in semitransparent patches on the leaves called windows [S3]. Leaves with windowing and shot holes are caused by early instars of FAW [S4].

The sawdust-like material in the middle of maize plants is frass, caterpillar poo from Fall Armyworm. Large quantities of frass are present and when it dries it resembles sawdust [S2]. Whorl damage assessment notes frass with a sawdust-like appearance [S5].
You usually find only one or two caterpillars per whorl because larger Fall Armyworm larvae become cannibalistic and eat each other to reduce competition for food [S1].
Under warm conditions, a female moth can lay 6 to 10 egg masses of 100 to 300 eggs each, giving a maximum of 1 500 to 2 000 eggs in her lifetime of 2-3 weeks [S2]
Fall Armyworm is an insect pest of more than 80 plant species, causing damage to economically important cultivated cereals such as maize, rice, sorghum, and also to vegetable crops and cotton [S2].

Fall Armyworm damage shows leaves with windowing and shot holes from early instars, extensive defoliation with fresh frass in the whorl and no dead heart, and defoliation by larvae in the whorl [S1]. Stem borer damage shows typical leaf surface feeding by young caterpillars, a hole where older caterpillars bore into the maize stem, and deadheart caused by feeding inside stems of young plants [S1].

Sesamia calamistis is described in the guide and its infestation is contrasted with Fall Armyworm infestation [S6]. The maize stem borer Busseola fusca is noted as a maize pest in Africa where Bt maize has been deployed and resistance has been observed [S4].

African Armyworm is native to Africa and faces a complex of natural biological enemies such as predators, parasitoids, diseases. FAW probably arrived in Africa unaccompanied by its natural enemies, allowing populations to increase more unchecked than normal [S1]

Maize damaged by Fall Armyworm is not made unsafe to eat by direct damage from the pest, although infested ears are usually not consumed by humans and damage can make maize more susceptible to aflatoxin presence [S1].

Heavy leaf eating by Fall Armyworm can cause yield loss, especially in early vegetative stage, but maize plants can significantly recover and compensate from early growth stage leaf damage and short duration defoliation. Total loss of the harvest is not typical; FAW mostly eats leaves and direct damage does not affect food safety [S1][S3]

Fall armyworm damage is most serious when larger caterpillars are in the whorl, and feeding on young plants can kill the growing point. By stages 3-6 the caterpillar reaches the protective whorl region where it does the most damage, resulting in ragged holes in the leaves. Feeding on young plants can kill the growing point resulting in no new leaves or cobs developing. [S4]

Push-pull is a habitat management strategy that uses plant diversity to manage Fall Armyworm in maize. It is a pesticide free technology that conserves natural enemies thereby increasing their abundance, diversity and activity [S2]. The technology appears effective in controlling Fall Armyworm and other lepidopteran pests compared to maize mono cropping systems, with associated maize grain yield increases under the conditions tested [S1][S2]. It is a specific application illustrating the general principle of the role of plant diversity on insect populations [S1].

The Economic Threshold Level is an attempt to improve decision making when deciding whether a pesticide should be sprayed. The ETL states that a certain pest density for example number of infested plants will lead to a yield loss. This yield loss that will occur at the end of the season has a cost which equals costs of treatment. The ETL is computed usually based on three parameters using the following equation: ETL = management costs USD/ha or cost in local currency/ha commodity price USD/kg X damage coefficient the expected yield loss at the ETL pest density kg/ha/#pest/ha [S2].

Cassava mosaic disease is mainly spread through primary infection when planting already infected cassava cuttings. In a small percentage of cases it is spread from plant to plant by the whitefly vector [S1].
Cassava mosaic disease can cause production losses of between 50 and 90 percent [S2]. In Kenya a severe form caused yield losses of 80–100 percent in farmers’ fields [S1].

Cassava mosaic disease spreads mainly through planting already infected cassava cuttings. Infected planting material leads to an infected plant and severity increases from one generation to the next. Use virus-free planting material and use resistant or tolerant cultivars. Research programmes have developed new varieties with resistance or tolerance to the new strain of CMD and efforts continue to multiply planting materials and make them available to farmers. Field schools link up with programmes that distribute disease-tolerant cassava varieties and test them in multiplication fields. Two key recommendations for control are adoption of appropriate cultural practices, especially the use of resistant or tolerant cultivars and virus-free planting material. [S1][S5][S3][S4][S6]
Cassava from plants with mosaic or brown streak disease does not pose problems for human health [S4]; roots can still be used if the infection is not too severe [S2].

Phytosanitation is the elimination and destruction of all diseased plants that occur in a field to remove all sources of contamination so that plants can produce healthy planting material and the farmer can have a healthy crop [S1]. It is the uprooting of diseased materials [S4].

In a cassava multiplication field phytosanitation must be done regularly throughout the cropping cycle, and eliminated plants are not replaced. The optimal frequency is once a week for the first two months of the crop once the gaps have been filled, and every two weeks for the rest of the cropping cycle until harvesting of the cuttings [S2][S4].

Uproot and destroy the whole plant and all plants that have symptoms of disease [S2]. Phytosanitation involves to localize, uproot and destroy all plants with symptoms of diseases or other atypical characteristics [S6].

No, you cannot go straight from a regular production field into the multiplication field to do phytosanitation. After visiting a regular production field, one cannot go to the multiplication field to do phytosanitation [S1].

Bacterial blight begins with jagged spots with a watery (oily) appearance on the leaves, which slowly wilt until they become dry and eventually fall. A gum is secreted on the petioles and young stems [S1].

Some farmers believe thunder to be the cause, but bacterial blight is a disease spread by bacteria (microbes). The bacteria can be found in the gums secreted by the plant and live in the plant’s interior; plant cuttings are the biggest source of contamination. The disease spreads easily when climate conditions are favourable, such as humidity and heat, and is spread by rain splashing, tools, animals and humans [S1][S3]

Bacterial blight is spread by rain splashing, by tools such as machete hoe clippers etc., by animals and by humans. Bacteria can be found in the gums secreted by the plant and plant cuttings are the biggest source of contamination. [S3]

Bacterial blight spreads easily when climate conditions are favourable with humidity and heat [S2]. It develops well during periods of high temperature and high air humidity [S4]. It develops well during warm and humid periods, and periods of strong rain result in high air humidity [S4]. The experiment is done during a warm and humid period [S1].

Bacterial blight spreads by rain splash, tools such as machete hoe clippers, animals and humans, and plant cuttings are the biggest source of contamination because bacteria live inside the plant [S3]. Use healthy plant cuttings to limit contamination [S3]. Use resistant or tolerant varieties; a tolerant variety can react by growing new shoots from the base of the plant [S1][S3]. Adopt improved techniques: plant when rains occur, apply good fertilization, and avoid competition with weeds [S3]. The disease is worse in marginal conditions where soil is poor or weed competition is high [S3].

Anthracnose is a fungal disease. The cankers are caused by a fungus which begins with wounds caused by the stings of an insect named Pseudotheraptus devastans; the development of the secondary infection, anthracnose disease, is entirely dependent on the insect stings [S1].

Anthracnose is a fungal disease of cassava. It is characterized by the presence of cankers (lesions) on the stem and at the base of the petioles of the leaves [S1]. The cankers can grow deeply and reach the central part of the stem, causing it to break easily [S1]. The disease can disturb the circulation of plant sap, blocking the feeding of the upper part until the leaves fall off and the stem dries up [S1]. The plant tops can look dead [S1].

Anthracnose can disturb the circulation of plant sap, blocking the feeding of the upper part until the leaves fall off and the stem dries up. The result is that the plant tops look dead, leading the disease to be confused with bacterial blight [S2].
Leaf spots occur on old leaves and the economic impact of the disease is therefore limited [S1].
Leaf spots on cassava are caused by Cercosporiosis [S1].
It is cassava mealy bug. The mealy bug appears as a white mass/white floury mass during the dry season that covers the insects and their eggs on shoots [S1][S2]

It was brought under control following research to introduce and release a parasitic wasp (Apoanagyris lopezi) that lays its eggs in the mealy bug. Its larvae develop in the mealy bug and kill it. It is efficient at keeping populations of cassava mealy bug in check in most situations. [S1][S5]
The cassava mealy bug appears principally in the dry season [S1]. It is not very visible during the rainy season [S2]. It disappears during the rainy season when it gets washed off by the rain [S1].

Use resistant varieties. Plant at the beginning of the rainy season. Use good fertilization. Adopt improved cultural practices. Use biological control. A parasitic wasp Apoanagyris lopezi lays its eggs in the mealy bug and its larvae develop in the mealy bug and kill it [S1][S2][S5].
The eggs and young mealy bugs are easily transported by wind and rain, cassava cuttings, animals and humans, spreading to contaminate other plants and fields [S2].

At present, there are no efficient management methods for controlling root scale insects. A moderately long fallow period (3–5 years) combined with deep soil preparation can help reduce the level of infestation [S1].

Small yellow spots and leaf curling in the dry season are described for green spidermite and are symptoms easily confused with those of mosaic virus. During the dry season one can observe chlorosis in the form of small spots, as well as leaves curling – symptoms easily confused with those of mosaic virus. Upon closer examination with a magnifying glass, it is possible to observe small green spidermites on the underside of the leaves [S1]. The passages do not allow a definite diagnosis from description alone; check the underside of leaves with a magnifying glass for small green spidermites and contact your local extension officer for field confirmation.
Green spidermites are found on the underside of cassava leaves [S1][S2].

You can manage green spidermite with several approaches. Use resistant varieties. Plant at the beginning of the rainy season. Use good fertilization. Use improved cultural practices. Use biological control with T. aripo as a predator, which feeds on the green spidermite and keeps populations low [S3].

Green spidermite feeds on leaves and destroys the plant’s potential chlorophyll [S1]. It feeds by sucking and injects a toxin [S3]. Attacks can slow down or even halt plant growth and cause retarded growth with shorter / reduced internodes at terminal parts, an effect which remains even after recovery [S1][S3]. Strong infestations can lead to dropping of young leaves [S3]. During dry season it causes chlorosis in the form of small spots and leaves curling [S3].

Locate the hole or route of the tunnel excavated by the mole rat. Place hot pepper, dry cow dung and cotton wool at the entrance to the tunnel. Burn the hot pepper, dry cow dung and cotton wool. Drive the smoke into the tunnel as a blacksmith does. The smoke of hot pepper, dry cow dung and cotton wool is known to drive away the mole rat. [S1]
The mole rat can consume up to 50 percent of the cassava in the field [S1].

The Tshokwe tribe experience with hills to ridge up cassava plants gives satisfactory results in mole control, and a field study is proposed to test soil preparation with ridges, with hills, and for direct planting to help farmers adapt a soil preparation method to reduce damage by moles [S1]

A good cassava cutting is taken from the sufficiently hardened median part of the stem, not the top and bottom parts. The cutting should be 15–25 cm long with a minimum of 4–5 eyes. Attention needs to be paid to the length of the cuttings, any bruising of or damage to the epidermis and buds, and damage caused by termites. The quality of the cuttings affects establishment, growth performance and, ultimately, yield. [S6]
